{{Short description|Stochastic process}}
In [[probability theory]], a '''branching random walk''' is a [[stochastic process]] that generalizes both the concept of a [[random walk]] and of a [[branching process]].  At every generation (a [[discrete time|point of discrete time]]), a branching random walk's value is a set of elements that are located in some [[linear space]], such as the [[real line]]. Each element of a given generation can have several descendants in the next generation. The location of any descendant is the sum of its parent's location and a [[random variable]].

This process is a spatial expansion of the [[Galton–Watson process]].<ref>{{Cite journal |last=Kaplan |first=Norman |date=1982 |title=A Note on the Branching Random Walk |url=https://www.jstor.org/stable/3213494 |journal=Journal of Applied Probability |volume=19 |issue=2 |pages=421–424 |doi=10.2307/3213494 |issn=0021-9002|url-access=subscription }}</ref> Its continuous equivalent is called branching Brownian motion.<ref>{{Cite book |last=Shi |first=Zhan |url=https://link.springer.com/book/10.1007/978-3-319-25372-5 |title=Branching Random Walks |publisher=[[Springer Science+Business Media|Springer]] |year=2015 |isbn=978-3-319-25371-8 |series=École d’Été de Probabilités de Saint-Flour XLII – 2012 |volume=2151 |location=Paris |language=en |doi=10.1007/978-3-319-25372-5 |issn=0075-8434}}</ref><ref>{{Citation |chapter=Branching Brownian Motion |date=2016 |title=Gaussian Processes on Trees: From Spin Glasses to Branching Brownian Motion |pages=60–75 |editor-last=Bovier |editor-first=Anton |chapter-url=https://www.cambridge.org/core/books/abs/gaussian-processes-on-trees/branching-brownian-motion/69F2EF3DEC5313EBB0A726B0D30D5AEA |access-date=2024-11-25 |series=Cambridge Studies in Advanced Mathematics |place=Cambridge |publisher=Cambridge University Press |isbn=978-1-107-16049-1}}</ref>

[[File:Branching random walk example.svg|thumb|Example of a branching random walk]]

==Example==
An example of branching random walk can be constructed where the branching process generates exactly two descendants for each element, a ''binary ''branching random walk. Given the [[initial condition]] that ''X''<sub>ϵ</sub>&nbsp;=&nbsp;0, we suppose that ''X''<sub>1</sub> and ''X''<sub>2</sub> are the two children of ''X''<sub>ϵ</sub>. Further, we suppose that they are [[independence (probability theory)|independent]] [[normal distribution|{{mathcal|N}}(0,&nbsp;1)]] random variables.  Consequently, in generation&nbsp;2, the random variables ''X''<sub>1,1</sub> and ''X''<sub>1,2</sub> are each the sum of ''X''<sub>1</sub> and a {{mathcal|N}}(0,&nbsp;1) random variable. In the next generation, the random variables ''X''<sub>1,2,1</sub> and ''X''<sub>1,2,2</sub> are each the sum of ''X''<sub>1,2</sub> and a {{mathcal|N}}(0,&nbsp;1) random variable. The same construction produces the values at successive times.

Each lineage in the infinite "genealogical tree" produced by this process, such as the sequence ''X''<sub>ϵ</sub>, ''X''<sub>1</sub>, ''X''<sub>1,2</sub>, ''X''<sub>1,2,2</sub>, ..., forms a conventional random walk.
